src/graphics.loft

// Copyright (c) 2026 Jurjen Stellingwerff
// SPDX-License-Identifier: LGPL-3.0-or-later
// graphics — a 2-D pixel canvas, and the window/GPU layer under it.
//
// TWO HALVES, and which one you want decides everything else.  The `Canvas` half
// is a flat vector of packed RGBA integers: it needs no window, no driver and no
// GL context, so it runs under `loft test` and answers questions about pixels.
// The `gl_*` half is the real window — shaders, VBOs, framebuffers — and every
// one of those is a native call that answers *"native function not loaded"* where
// there is no context.  Write the drawing against `Canvas` and it stays testable.
//
// ── Using it ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
//
//     cv = graphics::canvas(64, 48, graphics::rgb(20, 20, 30));
//     cv.fill_rect(8, 8, 20, 12, graphics::rgb(200, 60, 40));
//     cv.draw_line(0, 0, 63, 47, graphics::rgb(255, 255, 255));
//
//     // Alpha COMPOSITES; `set_pixel` would have replaced instead.
//     cv.blend_pixel(10, 10, graphics::rgba(0, 0, 255, 128));
//     px = cv.get_pixel(10, 10);          // -> r 99, g 29, b 147, a 255:
//                                         //    half the red rect, half the blue
//     cv.save_png("out.png");
//
// ⚠ COLOUR IS 0xAARRGGBB, so a bare `0xFF0000` literal is red at alpha ZERO and
// composites to nothing.  `rgb()` is the same pack with alpha 255 — reach for it
// rather than for a literal, and `color_r`/`_g`/`_b`/`_a` take the channels back
// out.
//
// The rest of the canvas surface is more primitives at the same level: lines,
// rects, circles, ellipses, beziers, an anti-aliased line, triangles and
// polygons, plus two resamplers (`resize_lanczos`, `resize_bicubic`).  The `gl_*`
// surface below them mirrors the OpenGL calls it wraps, and `stage` is the
// retained scene that drives either half.

use mesh3d::*;
use glb::*;
use imaging;

// RGBA color packed as a single integer: 0xAARRGGBB.
// Alpha: 255 = fully opaque, 0 = fully transparent.
// Use rgba() to construct and r()/g()/b()/a() to extract channels.

// Pack RGBA channels into a single integer using bitwise ops.
// Layout: bits 24..31 = alpha, 16..23 = red, 8..15 = green, 0..7 = blue.
// Loft integers are 64-bit signed post-2c, so the packed value fits
// directly — no widening cast needed.  Each channel is MASKED to 8 bits, so an
// out-of-range argument wraps rather than saturating or being refused.
// Example: @GFX-001 — the alpha byte is the one a hand-written hex literal
// leaves at zero, and a zero alpha is fully transparent.
pub fn rgba(cr: integer, cg: integer, cb: integer, ca: integer) -> integer {
  ((ca & 255) << 24) | ((cr & 255) << 16) | ((cg & 255) << 8) | (cb & 255)
}

// Opaque colour: the same pack with alpha 255.  `rgb(255, 0, 0)` is 0xFFFF0000 —
// NOT the 0xFF0000 a reader reaches for, which has alpha 0.
// Example: @GFX-001 — why the literal and this call are different colours, and
// what each compositing path does with the difference.
pub fn rgb(cr: integer, cg: integer, cb: integer) -> integer {
  rgba(cr, cg, cb, 255)
}

// The channels back out of a packed colour, matching `rgba`'s layout — red,
// green, blue, then alpha off the high byte.
pub fn color_r(color: integer) -> integer { (color >> 16) & 255 }
// Green.
pub fn color_g(color: integer) -> integer { (color >> 8) & 255 }
// Blue.
pub fn color_b(color: integer) -> integer { color & 255 }
// Alpha.  255 is opaque; a colour written as a bare 0xRRGGBB literal reads 0
// here, which is what makes it composite to nothing.
pub fn color_a(color: integer) -> integer {
  // integer is i64 post-2c, so the shift is logical on the high byte.
  ((color & 0xFF000000) >> 24) & 255
}

// A 2D pixel canvas backed by a flat vector of RGBA integers.
// Pixels are stored row-major: data[y * width + x].
pub struct Canvas {
  pub const width: integer,
  pub const height: integer,
  pub const data: vector<integer>
}

// `count` copies of `value`, built by doubling rather than one element
// at a time.
//
// A comprehension — `[for _ in 0..count { value }]` — emits three
// bytecodes per element (allocate the slot, write it, bump the length),
// so a 960x720 pixel buffer costs about 2.07 million dispatches.
// Appending a vector to ITSELF is a single block copy, so doubling
// reaches `count` in roughly log2(count) of them.
//
// Walking the bits of `count` from the top — double, then append one
// element where that bit is set — lands on `count` EXACTLY, which is
// what makes this usable: no overshoot to trim, and no tail loop.
// A prefix-slice variant was measured too and is both slower (51 ms)
// and wrong at count = 0.
//
// Measured on the interpreter, count = 691 200 (one 960x720 frame):
// 177 ms -> 10 ms, a factor of 17.  Sizes 0, 1, 9 216, 65 537 and
// 691 200 all match the comprehension element for element.
fn filled(count: integer, value: integer) -> vector<integer> {
  fi_out: vector<integer> = [];
  if count <= 0 { return fi_out; }
  // Highest set bit of `count`.
  fi_top = 0;
  while (count >> (fi_top + 1)) != 0 { fi_top = fi_top + 1; }
  fi_i = fi_top;
  while fi_i >= 0 {
    fi_out += fi_out;
    if ((count >> fi_i) & 1) == 1 { fi_out += [value]; }
    fi_i = fi_i - 1;
  }
  fi_out
}

// Create a canvas filled with a solid color.
pub fn canvas(cw: integer, ch: integer, fill_color: integer) -> Canvas {
  // Build `data` inside the literal so the const field is set once at
  // construction (was a post-literal `result.data = …` fill).
  Canvas { width: cw, height: ch, data: filled(cw * ch, fill_color) }
}

// Get pixel color at (x, y). Returns 0 if out of bounds — and 0 is a COLOUR the
// canvas can hold (`rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)`), so the answer cannot serve as a bounds
// test.  Bound with `width`/`height`.
// Example: @GFX-003 — a neighbourhood scan that tests the returned colour
// miscounts its own transparent pixels as off-canvas.
pub fn get_pixel(self: const Canvas, gx: integer, gy: integer) -> integer {
  if gx < 0 or gx >= self.width or gy < 0 or gy >= self.height {
    0
  } else {
    gp_idx = gy * self.width + gx;
    gp_d = &self.data;
    if gp_idx < len(gp_d) { gp_d[gp_idx] ?? 0 } else { 0 }
  }
}

// Set pixel color at (x, y). No-op if out of bounds.  STORES the colour byte for
// byte, alpha included — it does not composite; `blend_pixel` does.
// Example: @GFX-002 — storing a half-transparent colour replaces what was under
// it, rather than showing through it.
// Example: @GFX-003 — an out-of-range coordinate is declined in silence, so a
// wrong index is a missing part of the drawing, never a message.
pub fn set_pixel(self: Canvas, sx: integer, sy: integer, color: integer) {
  if sx >= 0 and sx < self.width and sy >= 0 and sy < self.height {
    sp_idx = sy * self.width + sx;
    sp_d = &self.data;
    if sp_idx < len(sp_d) {
      sp_d[sp_idx] = color;
    }
  }
}

// Fill the entire canvas with a solid color.
pub fn clear(self: Canvas, color: integer) {
  cl_n = self.data.len();
  for cl_i in 0..cl_n {
    self.data[cl_i] = color;
  }
}

// Alpha-blend src over dst. Both are 0xAARRGGBB packed integers.
// Uses standard "src over" compositing: out = src * alpha + dst * (1 - alpha).
pub fn blend(dst: integer, src: integer) -> integer {
  sa = color_a(src);
  if sa == 255 { return src; }
  if sa == 0 { return dst; }
  inv = 255 - sa;
  br = (color_r(src) * sa + color_r(dst) * inv) / 255;
  bg = (color_g(src) * sa + color_g(dst) * inv) / 255;
  bb = (color_b(src) * sa + color_b(dst) * inv) / 255;
  ba = sa + (color_a(dst) * inv) / 255;
  rgba(br, bg, bb, ba)
}

// Draw a pixel with alpha blending at (x, y) — the compositing counterpart to
// `set_pixel`, and the one a caller reaching for alpha usually meant.
// Example: @GFX-002 — store versus composite, side by side.
pub fn blend_pixel(self: Canvas, bx: integer, by: integer, color: integer) {
  if bx >= 0 and bx < self.width and by >= 0 and by < self.height {
    bp_idx = by * self.width + bx;
    bp_d = &self.data;
    if bp_idx < len(bp_d) {
      bp_d[bp_idx] = blend(bp_d[bp_idx] ?? 0, color);
    }
  }
}

// Fill a rectangle with a solid color. Clipped to canvas bounds.  Like every
// solid primitive here it STORES the colour (see `set_pixel`); a rectangle drawn
// in a half-transparent colour is not a translucent overlay.
// Example: @GFX-002 — what the buffer holds afterwards.
pub fn fill_rect(self: Canvas, rx: integer, ry: integer, rw: integer, rh: integer, color: integer) {
  x0 = if rx < 0 { 0 } else { rx };
  y0 = if ry < 0 { 0 } else { ry };
  x1 = if rx + rw > self.width { self.width } else { rx + rw };
  y1 = if ry + rh > self.height { self.height } else { ry + rh };
  fr_d = &self.data;
  fr_n = len(fr_d);
  for fr_y in y0..y1 {
    for fr_x in x0..x1 {
      fr_idx = fr_y * self.width + fr_x;
      if fr_idx < fr_n {
        fr_d[fr_idx] = color;
      }
    }
  }
}

// Draw a horizontal line from (x0, y) to (x1, y). Clipped.  The end is
// EXCLUSIVE — `[x0, x1)` — and a reversed span draws nothing rather than being
// normalised.
// Example: @GFX-004 — where a span starts and stops, and what silence looks like.
pub fn hline(self: Canvas, hx0: integer, hx1: integer, hy: integer, color: integer) {
  if hy < 0 or hy >= self.height { return; }
  left = if hx0 < 0 { 0 } else { hx0 };
  right = if hx1 > self.width { self.width } else { hx1 };
  hl_d = &self.data;
  hl_n = len(hl_d);
  for hl_x in left..right {
    hl_idx = hy * self.width + hl_x;
    if hl_idx < hl_n {
      hl_d[hl_idx] = color;
    }
  }
}

// Draw a vertical line from (x, y0) to (x, y1). Clipped.  Exclusive end and
// no normalisation, exactly like `hline`.
// Example: @GFX-004 — the half-open span rule on both axes.
pub fn vline(self: Canvas, vx: integer, vy0: integer, vy1: integer, color: integer) {
  if vx < 0 or vx >= self.width { return; }
  top = if vy0 < 0 { 0 } else { vy0 };
  bottom = if vy1 > self.height { self.height } else { vy1 };
  vl_d = &self.data;
  vl_n = len(vl_d);
  for vl_y in top..bottom {
    vl_idx = vl_y * self.width + vx;
    if vl_idx < vl_n {
      vl_d[vl_idx] = color;
    }
  }
}

// Draw a rectangle outline (1px border). Clipped.  Built from four half-open
// spans, so (x, y, w, h) covers x .. x + w - 1 by y .. y + h - 1.
// Example: @GFX-004 — the exact pixels, and the hollow interior.
pub fn draw_rect(self: Canvas, drx: integer, dry: integer, drw: integer, drh: integer, color: integer) {
  self.hline(drx, drx + drw, dry, color);
  self.hline(drx, drx + drw, dry + drh - 1, color);
  self.vline(drx, dry, dry + drh, color);
  self.vline(drx + drw - 1, dry, dry + drh, color);
}

// --- GL2.2: Bresenham line drawing ---

// Draw a line from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) using Bresenham's algorithm.
// Handles all octants. Each pixel is set (no blending).
pub fn draw_line(self: Canvas, lx0: integer, ly0: integer, lx1: integer, ly1: integer, color: integer) {
  dx = if lx1 > lx0 { lx1 - lx0 } else { lx0 - lx1 };
  dy = if ly1 > ly0 { ly1 - ly0 } else { ly0 - ly1 };
  sx = if lx0 < lx1 { 1 } else { -1 };
  sy = if ly0 < ly1 { 1 } else { -1 };
  err = dx - dy;
  cx = lx0;
  cy = ly0;
  for _ in 0..dx + dy + 1 {
    self.set_pixel(cx, cy, color);
    if cx == lx1 and cy == ly1 { break; }
    e2 = 2 * err;
    if e2 > -dy {
      err -= dy;
      cx += sx;
    }
    if e2 < dx {
      err += dx;
      cy += sy;
    }
  }
}

// --- GL2.3: Circle and ellipse ---

// Draw a circle outline using the midpoint algorithm.
// Center at (cx, cy) with the given radius. Clipped via set_pixel.
pub fn draw_circle(self: Canvas, ccx: integer, ccy: integer, radius: integer, color: integer) {
  cx = 0;
  cy = radius;
  d = 1 - radius;
  for _ in 0..radius * 4 + 4 {
    if cx > cy { break; }
    // Draw all 8 octant-symmetric points.
    self.set_pixel(ccx + cx, ccy + cy, color);
    self.set_pixel(ccx - cx, ccy + cy, color);
    self.set_pixel(ccx + cx, ccy - cy, color);
    self.set_pixel(ccx - cx, ccy - cy, color);
    self.set_pixel(ccx + cy, ccy + cx, color);
    self.set_pixel(ccx - cy, ccy + cx, color);
    self.set_pixel(ccx + cy, ccy - cx, color);
    self.set_pixel(ccx - cy, ccy - cx, color);
    if d < 0 {
      d += 2 * cx + 3;
    } else {
      d += 2 * (cx - cy) + 5;
      cy -= 1;
    }
    cx += 1;
  }
}

// Fill a circle (solid disk). Center at (cx, cy), given radius.
pub fn fill_circle(self: Canvas, fcx: integer, fcy: integer, radius: integer, color: integer) {
  cx = 0;
  cy = radius;
  d = 1 - radius;
  for _ in 0..radius * 4 + 4 {
    if cx > cy { break; }
    self.hline(fcx - cx, fcx + cx + 1, fcy + cy, color);
    self.hline(fcx - cx, fcx + cx + 1, fcy - cy, color);
    self.hline(fcx - cy, fcx + cy + 1, fcy + cx, color);
    self.hline(fcx - cy, fcx + cy + 1, fcy - cx, color);
    if d < 0 {
      d += 2 * cx + 3;
    } else {
      d += 2 * (cx - cy) + 5;
      cy -= 1;
    }
    cx += 1;
  }
}

// Fill an axis-aligned ellipse (solid). Center (cx, cy), radii (rx, ry).
pub fn fill_ellipse(self: Canvas, fex: integer, fey: integer, ferx: integer, fery: integer, color: integer) {
  fe_x = 0;
  fe_y = fery;
  fe_rx2 = ferx * ferx;
  fe_ry2 = fery * fery;
  fe_d1 = fe_ry2 - fe_rx2 * fery + fe_rx2 / 4;
  for _ in 0..ferx + fery + 1 {
    if fe_ry2 * fe_x > fe_rx2 * fe_y { break; }
    self.hline(fex - fe_x, fex + fe_x + 1, fey + fe_y, color);
    self.hline(fex - fe_x, fex + fe_x + 1, fey - fe_y, color);
    if fe_d1 < 0 {
      fe_d1 += fe_ry2 * (2 * fe_x + 3);
    } else {
      fe_d1 += fe_ry2 * (2 * fe_x + 3) + fe_rx2 * (-2 * fe_y + 2);
      fe_y -= 1;
    }
    fe_x += 1;
  }
  fe_d2 = fe_ry2 * (fe_x * 2 + 1) * (fe_x * 2 + 1) / 4 + fe_rx2 * (fe_y - 1) * (fe_y - 1) - fe_rx2 * fe_ry2;
  for _ in 0..ferx + fery + 1 {
    if fe_y < 0 { break; }
    self.hline(fex - fe_x, fex + fe_x + 1, fey + fe_y, color);
    self.hline(fex - fe_x, fex + fe_x + 1, fey - fe_y, color);
    if fe_d2 > 0 {
      fe_d2 += fe_rx2 * (-2 * fe_y + 3);
    } else {
      fe_d2 += fe_ry2 * (2 * fe_x + 2) + fe_rx2 * (-2 * fe_y + 3);
      fe_x += 1;
    }
    fe_y -= 1;
  }
}

// Draw an axis-aligned ellipse outline. Center (cx, cy), radii (rx, ry).
pub fn draw_ellipse(self: Canvas, ecx: integer, ecy: integer, erx: integer, ery: integer, color: integer) {
  // Midpoint ellipse algorithm — two regions.
  ex = 0;
  ey = ery;
  rx2 = erx * erx;
  ry2 = ery * ery;
  // Region 1: dy/dx > -1
  d1 = ry2 - rx2 * ery + rx2 / 4;
  for _ in 0..erx + ery + 1 {
    if ry2 * ex > rx2 * ey { break; }
    self.set_pixel(ecx + ex, ecy + ey, color);
    self.set_pixel(ecx - ex, ecy + ey, color);
    self.set_pixel(ecx + ex, ecy - ey, color);
    self.set_pixel(ecx - ex, ecy - ey, color);
    if d1 < 0 {
      d1 += ry2 * (2 * ex + 3);
    } else {
      d1 += ry2 * (2 * ex + 3) + rx2 * (-2 * ey + 2);
      ey -= 1;
    }
    ex += 1;
  }
  // Region 2: dy/dx <= -1
  d2 = ry2 * (ex * 2 + 1) * (ex * 2 + 1) / 4 + rx2 * (ey - 1) * (ey - 1) - rx2 * ry2;
  for _ in 0..erx + ery + 1 {
    if ey < 0 { break; }
    self.set_pixel(ecx + ex, ecy + ey, color);
    self.set_pixel(ecx - ex, ecy + ey, color);
    self.set_pixel(ecx + ex, ecy - ey, color);
    self.set_pixel(ecx - ex, ecy - ey, color);
    if d2 > 0 {
      d2 += rx2 * (-2 * ey + 3);
    } else {
      d2 += ry2 * (2 * ex + 2) + rx2 * (-2 * ey + 3);
      ex += 1;
    }
    ey -= 1;
  }
}

// --- GL2.4: Cubic Bezier curves ---

// Draw a cubic Bezier curve from (bx0,by0) to (bx3,by3) with control points
// (bx1,by1) and (bx2,by2). Uses adaptive subdivision — splits until segments
// are flat enough, then draws with Bresenham lines.
// Flatness threshold: max deviation of control points from the chord.
pub fn draw_bezier(self: Canvas, bx0: integer, by0: integer, bx1: integer, by1: integer, bx2: integer, by2: integer, bx3: integer, by3: integer, color: integer) {
  // Stack-based adaptive subdivision. Each segment = 8 entries (4 points × 2 coords).
  // Use a stack pointer (`bz_top`) with truncate-then-append on each
  // push so the lint sees only appends + slice reads, never indexed
  // writes — see the push site below.
  bz_sx: vector<integer> = [bx0, bx1, bx2, bx3];
  bz_sy: vector<integer> = [by0, by1, by2, by3];
  bz_top = 4;  // stack pointer = current vector length post-push
  for _ in 0..1000 {
    if bz_top == 0 { break; }
    // Pop segment (read 4 values, then decrease pointer).  `?? 0`
    // suppresses the OOB lint — `bz_top` is the stack pointer kept
    // invariantly >= 4 by the `break if bz_top == 0` guard above plus
    // the push-4-pop-4 protocol below.
    bz_p0x = bz_sx[bz_top - 4] ?? 0; bz_p1x = bz_sx[bz_top - 3] ?? 0;
    bz_p2x = bz_sx[bz_top - 2] ?? 0; bz_p3x = bz_sx[bz_top - 1] ?? 0;
    bz_p0y = bz_sy[bz_top - 4] ?? 0; bz_p1y = bz_sy[bz_top - 3] ?? 0;
    bz_p2y = bz_sy[bz_top - 2] ?? 0; bz_p3y = bz_sy[bz_top - 1] ?? 0;
    bz_top -= 4;
    // Flatness test: cross product distances of control points from chord
    bz_dx = bz_p3x - bz_p0x;
    bz_dy = bz_p3y - bz_p0y;
    bz_d1 = (bz_p1x - bz_p3x) * bz_dy - (bz_p1y - bz_p3y) * bz_dx;
    bz_d2 = (bz_p2x - bz_p3x) * bz_dy - (bz_p2y - bz_p3y) * bz_dx;
    if bz_d1 < 0 { bz_d1 = -bz_d1; }
    if bz_d2 < 0 { bz_d2 = -bz_d2; }
    bz_flat = if bz_d1 > bz_d2 { bz_d1 } else { bz_d2 };
    bz_chord2 = bz_dx * bz_dx + bz_dy * bz_dy;
    if bz_flat * bz_flat <= bz_chord2 or bz_chord2 == 0 {
      self.draw_line(bz_p0x, bz_p0y, bz_p3x, bz_p3y, color);
    } else {
      // de Casteljau subdivision at t=0.5
      bz_m01x = (bz_p0x + bz_p1x) / 2; bz_m01y = (bz_p0y + bz_p1y) / 2;
      bz_m12x = (bz_p1x + bz_p2x) / 2; bz_m12y = (bz_p1y + bz_p2y) / 2;
      bz_m23x = (bz_p2x + bz_p3x) / 2; bz_m23y = (bz_p2y + bz_p3y) / 2;
      bz_m012x = (bz_m01x + bz_m12x) / 2; bz_m012y = (bz_m01y + bz_m12y) / 2;
      bz_m123x = (bz_m12x + bz_m23x) / 2; bz_m123y = (bz_m12y + bz_m23y) / 2;
      bz_mx = (bz_m012x + bz_m123x) / 2; bz_my = (bz_m012y + bz_m123y) / 2;
      // Push second half first (so first half is popped next).
      // Truncate-then-append: the stack pointer `bz_top` is always
      // the next free slot; truncating to `bz_top` ensures `+=`
      // appends at that slot.  A vector keeps its own slice in place
      // (`v = v[0..n]`), so the pop costs no copy.
      bz_sx = bz_sx[0..bz_top];
      bz_sy = bz_sy[0..bz_top];
      bz_sx += [bz_mx, bz_m123x, bz_m23x, bz_p3x];
      bz_sy += [bz_my, bz_m123y, bz_m23y, bz_p3y];
      bz_top += 4;
      bz_sx += [bz_p0x, bz_m01x, bz_m012x, bz_mx];
      bz_sy += [bz_p0y, bz_m01y, bz_m012y, bz_my];
      bz_top += 4;
    }
  }
}

// --- GL2.6: Wu anti-aliased line ---

// Draw an anti-aliased line using Xiaolin Wu's algorithm.
// Uses blend_pixel for sub-pixel coverage.
pub fn draw_aa_line(self: Canvas, ax0: integer, ay0: integer, ax1: integer, ay1: integer, color: integer) {
  aa_dx = if ax1 > ax0 { ax1 - ax0 } else { ax0 - ax1 };
  aa_dy = if ay1 > ay0 { ay1 - ay0 } else { ay0 - ay1 };
  aa_steep = aa_dy > aa_dx;
  // If steep, we step along y instead of x.
  // Map to canonical form: always step along the longer axis.
  aa_x0 = if aa_steep { ay0 } else { ax0 };
  aa_y0 = if aa_steep { ax0 } else { ay0 };
  aa_x1 = if aa_steep { ay1 } else { ax1 };
  aa_y1 = if aa_steep { ax1 } else { ay1 };
  // Ensure we draw left-to-right
  if aa_x0 > aa_x1 {
    aa_tmp = aa_x0; aa_x0 = aa_x1; aa_x1 = aa_tmp;
    aa_tmp = aa_y0; aa_y0 = aa_y1; aa_y1 = aa_tmp;
  }
  aa_run = aa_x1 - aa_x0;
  if aa_run == 0 {
    // Single pixel
    self.set_pixel(ax0, ay0, color);
    return;
  }
  // Fixed-point gradient: rise * 256 / run.  `?? 0` suppresses the
  // div-by-zero lint — `aa_run == 0` is the vertical-line case
  // handled above with `set_pixel(...); return;`.  Parens scope `??`
  // to the div so the parser's null-fallback swap recognises it.
  aa_rise = aa_y1 - aa_y0;
  aa_grad256 = (aa_rise * 256 / aa_run) ?? 0;
  // y in fixed-point (8 fractional bits)
  aa_yf = aa_y0 * 256;
  aa_cr = graphics::color_r(color);
  aa_cg = graphics::color_g(color);
  aa_cb = graphics::color_b(color);
  for aa_xi in aa_x0..aa_x1 + 1 {
    aa_yi = aa_yf / 256;
    aa_frac = aa_yf - aa_yi * 256;
    if aa_frac < 0 { aa_frac += 256; aa_yi -= 1; }
    aa_a1 = 255 - aa_frac;
    aa_a2 = aa_frac;
    aa_c1 = graphics::rgba(aa_cr, aa_cg, aa_cb, aa_a1);
    aa_c2 = graphics::rgba(aa_cr, aa_cg, aa_cb, aa_a2);
    if aa_steep {
      self.blend_pixel(aa_yi, aa_xi, aa_c1);
      if aa_a2 > 0 { self.blend_pixel(aa_yi + 1, aa_xi, aa_c2); }
    } else {
      self.blend_pixel(aa_xi, aa_yi, aa_c1);
      if aa_a2 > 0 { self.blend_pixel(aa_xi, aa_yi + 1, aa_c2); }
    }
    aa_yf += aa_grad256;
  }
}

// --- GL2.5: Triangle fill (scanline) ---

// Fill a triangle with vertices (tx0,ty0), (tx1,ty1), (tx2,ty2).
// Uses flat-top/flat-bottom decomposition with scanline fill.
pub fn fill_triangle(self: Canvas, tx0: integer, ty0: integer, tx1: integer, ty1: integer, tx2: integer, ty2: integer, color: integer) {
  // Sort vertices by y: ta_y <= tb_y <= tc_y
  ta_x = tx0; ta_y = ty0;
  tb_x = tx1; tb_y = ty1;
  tc_x = tx2; tc_y = ty2;
  if ta_y > tb_y { tr_t = ta_x; ta_x = tb_x; tb_x = tr_t; tr_t = ta_y; ta_y = tb_y; tb_y = tr_t; }
  if tb_y > tc_y { tr_t = tb_x; tb_x = tc_x; tc_x = tr_t; tr_t = tb_y; tb_y = tc_y; tc_y = tr_t; }
  if ta_y > tb_y { tr_t = ta_x; ta_x = tb_x; tb_x = tr_t; tr_t = ta_y; ta_y = tb_y; tb_y = tr_t; }
  if ta_y == tc_y { return; }  // degenerate
  for tr_y in ta_y..tc_y + 1 {
    // x along edge A→C (the long edge, always valid).
    //
    // MULTIPLY BEFORE DIVIDING.  These are integers, so
    // `(tr_y - ta_y) / (tc_y - ta_y)` on its own is 0 on every
    // scanline but the last — which collapses the whole fill to a
    // vertical line at the apex plus the base row.  Scaling the run
    // first keeps the ratio's precision inside the integer divide.
    //
    // `?? 0` suppresses the div lint — `tc_y - ta_y != 0` is
    // guaranteed by the degenerate-triangle early-return above.
    // Parens scope `??` to just the div so the parser's null-fallback
    // swap fires.
    tr_xac = ta_x + ((tc_x - ta_x) * (tr_y - ta_y) / (tc_y - ta_y) ?? 0);
    // x along the short edge (A→B or B→C depending on scanline).
    // Both branches gate their divisor explicitly with the AND-side
    // `!= ta_y` / `!= tb_y` check, so `?? 0` is lint suppression.
    tr_xother = tr_xac;
    if tr_y < tb_y and tb_y != ta_y {
      tr_xother = ta_x + ((tb_x - ta_x) * (tr_y - ta_y) / (tb_y - ta_y) ?? 0);
    }
    if tr_y >= tb_y and tc_y != tb_y {
      tr_xother = tb_x + ((tc_x - tb_x) * (tr_y - tb_y) / (tc_y - tb_y) ?? 0);
    }
    if tr_y >= tb_y and tc_y == tb_y {
      tr_xother = tb_x;
    }
    tr_left = if tr_xac < tr_xother { tr_xac } else { tr_xother };
    tr_right = if tr_xac > tr_xother { tr_xac } else { tr_xother };
    self.hline(tr_left, tr_right + 1, tr_y, color);
  }
}

/// A point on the canvas, in pixels.
///
/// Exists because a polygon is a LIST of them and `fill_triangle`'s six loose
/// integers do not generalise — six is already the edge of what a caller gets
/// right in order, and a polygon has no fixed count.
///
/// NOT called `Point`: `mesh3d::LightType` has a `Point` variant and `graphics`
/// depends on mesh3d, so the name is taken and the collision is a hard error
/// ("struct 'Point' conflicts with a enumvalue of the same name"). `Vertex` is
/// mesh3d's too. Reach for `Coord` in 2-D graphics code and the 3-D names stay
/// where they belong.
pub struct Coord {
  pub px: integer,
  pub py: integer,
}

/// Fill a closed polygon under the EVEN-ODD rule.
///
/// The polygon closes itself: the last point joins the first, so a triangle is
/// three points and not four. Fewer than three points draws nothing.
///
/// Even-odd means a point is inside when a ray from it crosses the outline an odd
/// number of times, so a self-intersecting outline leaves its overlap EMPTY — the
/// classic five-point star is a pentagon-shaped hole with five filled arms. That
/// is a choice, not a bug: the alternative (non-zero winding) fills the middle,
/// and the two disagree on exactly the shapes people draw deliberately.
///
/// Matches `fill_triangle` pixel for pixel on a triangle, which is the reason the
/// row rule below is inclusive rather than the half-open rule a scanline filler
/// usually takes. See the note on `polygon_crossings`.
// Example: @GFX-006 — the star's hollow middle, and the triangle agreement.
pub fn fill_polygon(self: Canvas, pts: const vector<Coord>, color: integer) {
  fp_n = len(pts);
  if fp_n < 3 { return; }
  fp_top = pts[0]?.py;
  fp_bot = fp_top;
  for p in pts {
    if p.py < fp_top { fp_top = p.py; }
    if p.py > fp_bot { fp_bot = p.py; }
  }
  if fp_top < 0 { fp_top = 0; }
  if fp_bot >= self.height { fp_bot = self.height - 1; }
  for fp_y in fp_top..=fp_bot {
    fp_xs = polygon_crossings(pts, fp_y, fp_y == fp_bot);
    fp_i = 0;
    while fp_i + 1 < len(fp_xs) {
      // Inclusive span, like `fill_triangle`: `hline` takes a half-open end, so
      // the right edge is +1.
      self.hline(fp_xs[fp_i]?, fp_xs[fp_i + 1]? + 1, fp_y, color);
      fp_i += 2;
    }
  }
}

/// Where the outline crosses scanline `y`, left to right.
///
/// The rule is HALF-OPEN on an edge's lower end (`ylo <= y < yhi`) and that is
/// what makes even-odd work: a vertex the outline passes straight through belongs
/// to exactly one of its two edges, so it counts once. Count it twice — the
/// obvious inclusive rule — and a through-vertex yields two crossings at the same
/// x, which pair with each other and fill a single pixel where a whole span
/// belonged.
///
/// The cost is that the polygon's LOWEST row loses every edge, so `closing` turns
/// the rule inclusive for exactly that row. It is safe there and nowhere else: the
/// half-open rule exists to disambiguate a vertex the outline passes THROUGH, and
/// the extreme row has none — every edge meeting it goes back up, so no crossing
/// is counted twice. Measured: left half-open throughout, a triangle loses its
/// bottom vertex (1 px) or its whole base (34 px on a 34-wide one), which was the
/// entire `fill_triangle` disagreement.
fn polygon_crossings(pc_pts: const vector<Coord>, pc_y: integer,
                     closing: boolean) -> vector<integer> {
  pc_out: vector<integer> = [];
  pc_n = len(pc_pts);
  for i in 0..pc_n {
    pc_a = pc_pts[i]?;
    // `% pc_n` types nullable because a zero divisor answers null; `?? 0` names the
    // wrap target, which is where the last edge closes anyway.  The loop does not run
    // at all when `pc_n` is 0, so the default is unreachable rather than chosen.
    pc_b = pc_pts[(i + 1) % pc_n ?? 0]?;
    pc_ylo = if pc_a.py < pc_b.py { pc_a.py } else { pc_b.py };
    pc_yhi = if pc_a.py < pc_b.py { pc_b.py } else { pc_a.py };
    // A horizontal edge crosses no scanline: its endpoints are already carried by
    // the two edges that meet it, and counting it would flip parity along a row it
    // only touches.
    if pc_ylo == pc_yhi { continue }
    if pc_y < pc_ylo { continue }
    if pc_y > pc_yhi { continue }
    if pc_y == pc_yhi && !closing { continue }
    // Interpolate from the edge's TOP end, and multiply before dividing — the
    // same integer-precision rule `fill_triangle` documents.
    pc_ty = if pc_a.py < pc_b.py { pc_a } else { pc_b };
    pc_by = if pc_a.py < pc_b.py { pc_b } else { pc_a };
    pc_out += [pc_ty.px + ((pc_by.px - pc_ty.px) * (pc_y - pc_ty.py) / (pc_by.py - pc_ty.py) ?? 0)];
  }
  // Insertion sort: a crossing list is a handful of numbers, and a fresh vector
  // per scanline would cost more than the compare.
  for i in 1..len(pc_out) {
    pc_v = pc_out[i]?;
    pc_j = i;
    while pc_j > 0 && pc_out[pc_j - 1]? > pc_v {
      pc_out[pc_j] = pc_out[pc_j - 1]?;
      pc_j -= 1;
    }
    pc_out[pc_j] = pc_v;
  }
  pc_out
}

// ── Resampling ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────

/// Fixed-point fraction bits for resample weights — Pillow's `PRECISION_BITS`.
RESAMPLE_PREC = 22;
RESAMPLE_PI = 3.14159265358979323846;
BICUBIC_A = -0.5;

fn sinc_at(x: float) -> float {
  if x == 0.0 { return 1.0 }
  sc_xp = x * RESAMPLE_PI;
  (sin(sc_xp) / sc_xp)?
}

/// Pillow's bicubic kernel — the Keys cubic with `a = -0.5`, support 2.
///
/// The two branches are one polynomial each and the constant is the whole
/// identity of the filter: `a = -0.5` is Catmull-Rom, and another `a` is a
/// different picture, not a rounding difference.
fn bicubic_at(bc_x0: float) -> float {
  bc_x = if bc_x0 < 0.0 { -bc_x0 } else { bc_x0 };
  if bc_x < 1.0 { return ((BICUBIC_A + 2.0) * bc_x - (BICUBIC_A + 3.0)) * bc_x * bc_x + 1.0 }
  if bc_x < 2.0 { return (((bc_x - 5.0) * bc_x + 8.0) * bc_x - 4.0) * BICUBIC_A }
  0.0
}

/// The Lanczos-3 kernel: `sinc(x) * sinc(x/3)` inside a radius of 3, else 0.
fn lanczos_at(lz_x0: float) -> float {
  lz_x = if lz_x0 < 0.0 { -lz_x0 } else { lz_x0 };
  if lz_x < 3.0 { return sinc_at(lz_x) * sinc_at(lz_x / 3.0) }
  0.0
}

/// One axis of Pillow's `precompute_coeffs`, flattened into three parallel
/// vectors: each output index gets a window START, a TAP COUNT, and that many
/// fixed-point weights appended to `kk`.
///
/// The weights are normalised to sum to 1 in floating point and only then scaled
/// to integers, rounding AWAY from zero — both filters here have negative lobes,
/// and rounding them the same direction as the positive ones is what keeps the
/// taps summing back to `1 << RESAMPLE_PREC`.
///
/// `support0` and `filt` are the ONLY things that differ between Pillow's
/// filters, which is why they are parameters rather than two copies of this
/// function: the window arithmetic, the normalisation and the fixed-point
/// rounding are one derived fact and belong in one place.
fn resample_coeffs(in_size: integer, out_size: integer, support0: float,
                   filt: fn(float) -> float, starts: &vector<integer>,
                   counts: &vector<integer>, kk: &vector<integer>) {
  rc_scale = ((in_size as float) / (out_size as float))?;
  // Upscaling does not widen the kernel: the filter scale floors at 1.
  rc_fscale = if rc_scale < 1.0 { 1.0 } else { rc_scale };
  rc_support = support0 * rc_fscale;
  rc_ss = (1.0 / rc_fscale)?;
  for xx in 0..out_size {
    rc_centre = ((xx as float) + 0.5) * rc_scale;
    rc_min = (rc_centre - rc_support + 0.5) as integer;
    if rc_min < 0 { rc_min = 0; }
    rc_max = (rc_centre + rc_support + 0.5) as integer;
    if rc_max > in_size { rc_max = in_size; }
    rc_max -= rc_min;
    rc_row: vector<float> = [];
    rc_ww = 0.0;
    for x in 0..rc_max {
      rc_w = filt((((x + rc_min) as float) - rc_centre + 0.5) * rc_ss);
      rc_row += [rc_w];
      rc_ww += rc_w;
    }
    for x in 0..rc_max {
      rc_k = rc_row[x]?;
      if rc_ww != 0.0 { rc_k = (rc_k / rc_ww)?; }
      rc_scaled = rc_k * ((1 << RESAMPLE_PREC) as float);
      kk += [if rc_k < 0.0 { (rc_scaled - 0.5) as integer }
             else { (rc_scaled + 0.5) as integer }];
    }
    starts += [rc_min];
    counts += [rc_max];
  }
}

/// Fixed-point accumulator to a byte: shift the fraction off and clamp.
fn resample_clip(rq_v: integer) -> integer {
  rq_s = rq_v >> RESAMPLE_PREC;
  if rq_s < 0 { return 0 }
  if rq_s > 255 { return 255 }
  rq_s
}

/// Resample this canvas to `ow` x `oh` with a Lanczos-3 filter.
///
/// Byte-identical to Pillow's `Image.resize(..., Image.LANCZOS)`, which is the
/// point: the `.draw` corpus renders at 3x and downscales with exactly that, so a
/// renderer that resamples any other way cannot be pixel-compared against it
/// however good it looks (@PLN146 W0 finding 5).
///
/// **Alpha is premultiplied across the resample and undone after**, because
/// Pillow defines `resize` on an image with alpha as
/// `convert("RGBa") -> resize -> convert("RGBA")`. That is a contract, not an
/// optimisation: resampling straight RGBA lets a transparent texel's colour bleed
/// into its neighbours, and the two disagree on any edge where alpha varies.
/// Both roundings are Pillow's and neither is the obvious one — `(v*a + 127)/255`
/// going in, a TRUNCATING divide coming out, and alpha 0 passes its colour
/// through untouched rather than going black.
// Example: @GFX-007 — why a 3x supersample plus this is not the same picture as
// drawing once at final size.
pub fn resize_lanczos(self: const Canvas, ow: integer, oh: integer) -> Canvas {
  resample(self, ow, oh, 3.0, lanczos_at)
}

/// Resample with a BICUBIC filter — Pillow's `Image.resize` default.
///
/// The default is the reason this exists: `resize(size)` with no `resample=`
/// argument is bicubic, and code that builds a small image and enlarges it (a
/// gradient computed at 100x100, say) takes that path without naming it. Read
/// the call site's filter off the ARGUMENT LIST and it looks like there isn't
/// one.
///
/// ⚠ Bicubic has negative lobes, so an ENLARGEMENT overshoots: a hard 40→200
/// step upscaled 4x spans 28..212 in Pillow and here alike. That is the filter,
/// not a defect — clamping it away would be the defect.
pub fn resize_bicubic(self: const Canvas, ow: integer, oh: integer) -> Canvas {
  resample(self, ow, oh, 2.0, bicubic_at)
}

/// Pillow's two-pass resample, with the filter left to the caller.
///
/// One body, because the passes, the premultiply and the fixed-point
/// accumulation are the same derived fact for every filter — only the kernel and
/// its support differ.
fn resample(self: const Canvas, ow: integer, oh: integer, support0: float,
            filt: fn(float) -> float) -> Canvas {
  if ow < 1 || oh < 1 || self.width < 1 || self.height < 1 {
    return canvas(if ow < 1 { 1 } else { ow }, if oh < 1 { 1 } else { oh }, 0);
  }
  rl_iw = self.width;
  rl_ih = self.height;
  // Premultiplied channel planes, in Pillow's RGBA byte order.
  rl_pre: vector<integer> = [];
  for i in 0..(rl_iw * rl_ih) {
    rl_c = self.data[i]?;
    rl_a = (rl_c >> 24) & 255;
    rl_pre += [(((rl_c >> 16) & 255) * rl_a + 127) / 255 ?? 0,
               (((rl_c >> 8) & 255) * rl_a + 127) / 255 ?? 0,
               ((rl_c & 255) * rl_a + 127) / 255 ?? 0,
               rl_a];
  }
  hs: vector<integer> = []; hc: vector<integer> = []; hk: vector<integer> = [];
  resample_coeffs(rl_iw, ow, support0, filt, hs, hc, hk);
  rl_mid: vector<integer> = [];
  for _ in 0..(ow * rl_ih * 4) { rl_mid += [0]; }
  rl_base = 0;
  for xx in 0..ow {
    rl_xmin = hs[xx]?;
    rl_n = hc[xx]?;
    for yy in 0..rl_ih {
      for ch in 0..4 {
        rl_acc = 1 << (RESAMPLE_PREC - 1);
        for x in 0..rl_n {
          rl_acc += rl_pre[(yy * rl_iw + rl_xmin + x) * 4 + ch]? * hk[rl_base + x]?;
        }
        rl_mid[(yy * ow + xx) * 4 + ch] = resample_clip(rl_acc);
      }
    }
    rl_base += rl_n;
  }
  vs: vector<integer> = []; vc: vector<integer> = []; vk: vector<integer> = [];
  resample_coeffs(rl_ih, oh, support0, filt, vs, vc, vk);
  rl_out = canvas(ow, oh, 0);
  rl_od = &rl_out.data;
  rl_vbase = 0;
  for yy in 0..oh {
    rl_ymin = vs[yy]?;
    rl_n = vc[yy]?;
    for xx in 0..ow {
      rl_ch: vector<integer> = [];
      for ch in 0..4 {
        rl_acc = 1 << (RESAMPLE_PREC - 1);
        for y in 0..rl_n {
          rl_acc += rl_mid[((rl_ymin + y) * ow + xx) * 4 + ch]? * vk[rl_vbase + y]?;
        }
        rl_ch += [resample_clip(rl_acc)];
      }
      // Undo the premultiply and repack to 0xAARRGGBB.
      rl_a = rl_ch[3]?;
      rl_rgb: vector<integer> = [];
      for ch in 0..3 {
        rl_v = rl_ch[ch]?;
        if rl_a == 0 { rl_rgb += [rl_v]; }
        else {
          rl_u = (rl_v * 255) / rl_a ?? 0;
          rl_rgb += [if rl_u > 255 { 255 } else { rl_u }];
        }
      }
      rl_od[yy * ow + xx] = (rl_a << 24) | (rl_rgb[0]? << 16) | (rl_rgb[1]? << 8) | rl_rgb[2]?;
    }
    rl_vbase += rl_n;
  }
  rl_out
}

// Save canvas as a PNG file. Automatically uses RGBA if any pixel has alpha < 255,
// otherwise uses RGB. Returns true on success.
// Example: @GFX-005 — the choice is read off the pixels, so ONE alpha-0 pixel
// (a hand-written hex literal — @GFX-001) makes the whole file RGBA and that
// pixel a transparent hole.
//
// The PNG is imaging's (a C shim over lodepng), so it is the same file on every target.  A
// relative path resolves against the program's own directory, as loft's file I/O does.  False
// when the canvas is not whole (fewer pixels than width x height) or the file cannot be written.
pub fn save_png(self: const Canvas, path: text) -> boolean {
  n = self.width * self.height;
  if n <= 0 || len(self.data) < n { return false; }
  img = imaging::Image { name: path, width: self.width, height: self.height, data: [] };
  for i in 0..n {
    c = self.data[i] ?? 0;
    img.data += [imaging::Pixel { r: (c >> 16) & 255, g: (c >> 8) & 255, b: c & 255, a: (c >> 24) & 255 }];
  }
  img.save_png(path)
}

// --- The codes the window's calls take ---

// Capabilities for `Window.enable` / `Window.disable`.

pub const GL_BLEND = 2;

pub const DRAW_POINTS = 2;
